title_original: ‘I was very aggressive. They threw me out of every school’ … Julie Delpy on acting, anger and predatory directors
excerpt_original: Thirty years after the roles that made her famous, the star of Three Colours: White and the Before trilogy is busier than ever – as a screenwriter and director. But, she says, a lot of people have tried to keep her down To listen to Julie Delpy talk about her workload is to feel…

blocks.text: T o listen to Julie Delpy talk about her workload is to feel the need for a nap coming on. She is writing six screenplays at the moment that range from dark comedies to thrillers. “I don’t do monoculture,” she says. If her producer hadn’t reined her in, she would be working on five horror film scripts too.

The actor, writer and director says she doesn’t sleep well – she can sit at her desk for up to 18 hours, writing “until I run out of steam. I know you could think I’m exaggerating. I’m not. If you look at my computer, you will see how bad it is.” We’re on a video call, Delpy from her home in Los Angeles. She is charming – intense and funny in big black-framed glasses. “I look so weird with this angle on my hair,” she says, of the ceiling light behind her. “Like an angry bald man!”

Now 56, she has been working in film since she was a teenager, in a career that has spanned European arthouse (such as Krzysztof Kieślowski’s Three Colours: White, from 1994), romance (Richard Linklater’s Before trilogy, which began in 1995) and indies (Jim Jarmusch’s Broken Flowers, 2005). In 2015, she was even in Avengers: Age of Ultron.

blocks.alt: A blond woman sat at a wooden garden table, holding an orange flower and leaning her head on her hands
blocks.caption: ‘I was broken many times’ … Delpy. Photograph: Jessica Chou/The Guardian

blocks.text: As a writer and director, Delpy has made eight feature films, including 2 Days in Paris and its follow-up, 2 Days in New York. She is, by any measure, a Hollywood success, and yet she still has the feel of an outsider. She has been, she will say a little later, “broken many times” by the industry.

Now the comedy she directed and co-wrote, Meet the Barbarians, about a French village that takes in what local people believe will be a Ukrainian refugee family, only to find out they are Syrian, is being released in the US. The idea for the film came out of the 2015 refugee crisis, in which 1.4 million people arrived in Europe via the Mediterranean after fleeing the Middle East. She interviewed refugees and organisations that worked with them – many of whom spoke about Europe’s reluctance to make long-term plans for the people arriving on its shores. Since Russia invaded Ukraine, more than 4 million Ukrainian refugees have been granted temporary protection status to stay in the EU. She found the difference in approach to these two groups of people startling. “So many people I know [in Europe] were welcoming Ukrainian refugees, which is great. But I was like, wow, I’ve just interviewed hundreds of people that have been treated like shit, and no one would open their doors to them.”

blocks.alt: A blond woman wearing a yellow jacket on a bike cycling under a stone bridge
blocks.caption: Delpy in Meet the Barbarians (2024). Photograph: Album/Alamy

blocks.text: She is an immigrant herself, she says, having moved from her native France to the US in 1990, but, she points out: “I’m an immigrant who is blond with blue eyes.” She is lucky, she says, even if her husband, the production manager Dimitris Birbilis, who is Greek, has experienced more overt xenophobia: “I can feel that there are looks sometimes.” (She has a 17-year-old son with her previous partner, composer Marc Streitenfeld.) “We have legal papers, I’m an American, but you feel the tension.” Trump, she says, “has brought so much darkness to this country. He’s made people confident to say the most horrible things – racist, misogynist, homophobic things without feeling affected. It’s very disturbing.”

Politicians around the world, she believes, are “pushing their agenda of fear and fearmongering to get elected. Refugees don’t steal jobs. They don’t destroy the economy. All that is bullshit.” France is facing the possibility of a far-right president in Marine Le Pen next year. Delpy is off now, switching from lambasting the demonisation of “wokeism” to the distortion of “reality and truth, so much that it’s difficult to even talk about history or facts with some people”. She feels it’s a scary time. “The most unqualified people are in power around the world, and I’m terrified of that.”

Delpy’s parents were actors and have appeared in her films (her mother, Marie Pillet, died in 2009). Her father, Albert Delpy, played her fictional father in 2 Days in Paris and is also in Meet the Barbarians. Is he good at taking direction from her? “No. It’s like directing King Kong.” She laughs. “As he’s getting older, he’s getting sweeter. We used to have major fights, but now he’s such a good guy.” She describes a bohemian Parisian childhood. She didn’t like school. “I was very aggressive, so they threw me out of every school until I got out completely and became an actor,” she says.

She recently went back through some of her diaries and stories from working as a child actor, “just cleaning up, going through shit. It explained a lot for me. I realised how sensitive I was and how much I was putting on an armour to survive.” She found things she had written as a child actor, she says, “about this business and how creepy it was in France with directors”.

At 13, at an audition, she says she was alone with a director in his apartment when he asked her to take her clothes off. “I took the script and threw it in his face,” says Delpy. She told her parents. “I said: ‘I don’t want to be an actress if that’s what it means.’ And they were like: ‘Well, look at us. We didn’t do that.’”

blocks.alt: Three people stand with their arms around each other, posing for photos
blocks.caption: With her parents, Albert Delpy and Marie Pillet, in 2007. Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The Guardian

blocks.text: Other early experiences were better. Delpy’s first film role was in Jean-Luc Godard’s Detective. “It was great to work with him, and he was such a nice guy,” she says. “I mean, he was not a nice guy” – the influential French director was notoriously volatile and difficult – “but with me he was incredibly nice and respectful, and protective.”

But sexual harassment as a young woman in Hollywood was unavoidable. “I remember this guy, who’s still around, a very powerful guy. He tried to break into the bathroom where I was at a party.” She has spoken before about turning down a director’s sexual advances around the same time, when she was in her early 20s, and that he had spread word in the business that she was “difficult”. “The minute you say no to people …” She pauses. “And also the way I was expressing myself, I was very straightforward.”

When Harvey Weinstein’s company Miramax was involved in releasing the second part of the Three Colours trilogy, White, in which Delpy starred, she says she chose to stay in a different hotel from him because of the rumours she had heard. “I was not naive because I was coming from France, where it was like, you were dodging the paedophiles basically,” she says with a grim laugh. “I had the luck to not be a young girl from the midwest who has no idea what’s going on.”

Making Before Sunrise (1995), in which she plays Céline, a beautiful young free spirit who spends a night in Vienna with Jesse (Ethan Hawke), Delpy says she contributed many lines and ideas to the script and was frustrated that this wasn’t recognised with a writing credit. “I went through a really rough time in my late 20s but it took me reading my journal to actually know that. I was like: ‘Oh, that sounds like a breakdown.’” On the surface, she says, most people wouldn’t have known anything was wrong. “I wouldn’t cry and stay alone.” Instead, she felt a lot of anger. “I was doing quite a lot of drinking.”

blocks.alt: A young couple in a close embrace, looking into each other’s eyes
blocks.caption: ‘We’ll never know what happens to them’ … Delpy and Ethan Hawke in Before Sunrise (1995). Photograph: Album/Alamy

blocks.text: She was, however, along with Hawke, recognised as a writer on the sequel, Before Sunset , which was nominated for a best adapted screenplay Oscar. When Before Sunrise was released, she says, it wasn’t a big success. “It grew with the second film. Even when I was writing the second one, my agent fired me, saying I was wasting my time writing a sequel to a little indie film that no one gave a shit about, and I should be going on auditions instead of writing.”

Delpy doesn’t come across as bitter, but she is evidently still angry. “People have hurt me in this business,” she says. When I ask her to elaborate, she talks vaguely, mentioning people “telling me I was stupid. Trying to break my confidence.” Just a few years ago, she says, a financier pulled out of her sci-fi drama My Zoe at the last minute, put off, she believes, by someone briefing against her. “There’s still a system that’s trying to keep people where they want them to be,” she says.

blocks.alt: A blond woman wearing black glasses and a black jacket holding a mug in a room with a desk and plant behind her
blocks.caption: ‘I was very straightforward’ … Delpy. Photograph: Jessica Chou/The Guardian

blocks.text: Delpy always wanted to write and direct, and she made her first film, Blah Blah Blah, a short that was shown at Sundance, in 1995. She never wanted to be typecast as the ingenue. “I was able to get out of that pretty quickly,” she says. It became even more important to create her own work as she got older in an industry where good parts for middle-aged actors are still scarce. Twenty years ago, it was even worse. “Yeah, I didn’t love some of the stuff, so I started writing.” She created and starred in the 2021 Netflix series On the Verge, about the lives of four women in their late 40s, but it lasted for only one season. “I don’t know what happened,” she says, but “the algorithm doesn’t love women in that age group apparently”.

Next year Delpy is in a Ruben Östlund comedy with Keanu Reeves, The Entertainment System Is Down, and in actor Sonoya Mizuno’s directorial debut, Stages, about a young dancer at an elite ballet school. She is regularly asked about a fourth Before film but says 2013’s Before Midnight is the last one. “Richard approached us at one point, but the idea didn’t really go very far.” Reportedly, her character, Céline, was going to die. “I wasn’t into it. Ethan was not really into it, and Richard was not really into it. Nobody liked it.” She laughs. “Now we’ve passed the time that we were supposed to do it. It’s a trilogy. We’ll never know what happens to them.”

blocks.alt: Blond woman wearing black gloves, places a hand on a window, and looks solemn
blocks.caption: As Dominique Vidal in Three Colours: White (1994). Photograph: Cinetext/Le Studio Canal+/Allstar

blocks.text: Does she feel – as I do when I watch those films – sad and wistful for the feeling of time passing, and what might have been? No, says Delpy, “I’m really excited about the future.” She says it was good to revisit the journals of her childhood and youth, “but now I’ve done it, I’m focusing on stuff I’m writing”. Those six (and counting) screenplays are calling and she’s energised because she thinks they are among her best work. It’s all she can do not to become completely consumed by them.

She says she has to make an effort to see people, “because I’m so happy in my world. You create a world and you live in it. I know it’s a film, but it’s also like jumping into a parallel universe. It’s the most fun thing in the world. I love making films because what was only in your head becomes something tangible.” She pauses. “I’m not saying all of this is great. A lot of it might end up turning shit, right? But, you know, I’m doing it anyway.”
